facts.statement: Effigia lived during the Late Triassic period.
Effigia fossils are known from the Late Triassic of New Mexico in the southwestern USA.
facts.quote: Effigia is an extinct genus of shuvosaurid known from the Late Triassic of New Mexico, south-western USA.

facts.statement: Effigia had a bipedal stance, a long neck, and a toothless beaked skull that resembled Cretaceous ornithomimid dinosaurs.
facts.quote: With a bipedal stance, long neck, and a toothless beaked skull, Effigia and other shuvosaurids bore a resemblance to the ornithomimid dinosaurs of the Cretaceous Period.

facts.statement: Effigia was a poposauroid pseudosuchian whose closest living relatives are crocodilians, not dinosaurs.
facts.quote: However, shuvosaurids were not dinosaurs, but were instead a specialized family of poposauroid pseudosuchians, meaning that their closest living relatives are crocodilians.

facts.statement: The holotype fossil of Effigia was collected by Edwin H. Colbert in 1947.
facts.quote: The holotype fossil was collected by Edwin H. Colbert in 1947.

facts.statement: Edwin H. Colbert collected the fossil blocks intending to find Coelophysis and believed no other large vertebrates were present.
facts.quote: Colbert's expedition intended to recover abundant fossils of the basal theropod dinosaur Coelophysis, and he believed that no other large vertebrates were present in the quarry.

facts.statement: Effigia okeeffeae was named by Nesbitt and Mark Norell in January 2006 in honor of Georgia O'Keeffe.
facts.quote: Nesbitt and Mark Norell, curator at the museum, named it Effigia okeeffeae in January 2006 after Georgia O'Keeffe, who spent many years at Ghost Ranch.

facts.statement: Effigia was a 2-meter-long animal recovered from Ghost Ranch quarry blocks excavated between 1947 and 1948.
facts.quote: Este animal de 2 metros de longitud fue recuperado por Edwin H. Colbert en bloques de roca de la cantera de Ghost Ranch, que fueron excavados entre 1947 y 1948.

facts.statement: The species was named in January 2006 after Georgia O'Keeffe, whose ashes were scattered at Ghost Ranch.
facts.quote: Nesbitt y Mark Norell, curador del museo, lo denominaron Effigia okeeffeae en enero de 2006 en honor de Georgia O'Keeffe, quien pasó muchos años en Ghost Ranch (y cuyas cenizas fueron esparcidas allí).

facts.statement: The resemblance of Effigia to ornithomimid dinosaurs is an example of extreme convergent evolution.
facts.quote: Its similarity to ornithomimids represents a case of "extreme" convergent evolution.

facts.statement: A 2007 proposal to synonymize Effigia with Shuvosaurus was not accepted by Nesbitt.
facts.quote: In 2007, Lucas and others suggested that "Effigia" was synonymous with "Shuvosaurus" and used the new combination "Shuvosaurus okeeffeae" for the animal. This proposal has not been accepted by Nesbitt.

facts.statement: Biomechanical studies indicate Effigia could not peck for food like ostriches because its skull could not withstand such forces.
facts.quote: It was previously suggested that it pecked for food like ostriches or other ratites, but biomechanical studies have estimated that its skull could not withstand such forces.

facts.statement: Effigia belongs to the family Poposauridae.
Effigia is classified within the unranked order Crurotarsi.
Effigia is classified within the order Rauisuchia.
Effigia lived during the Upper Triassic.
Effigia lived from 205.7 to 201.4 million years ago during the Rhaetian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Rhaetian to Rhaetian (205.7 to 201.4 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The holotype specimen was uncovered by graduate student Sterling Nesbitt in 2004 at the American Museum of Natural History.
rejected.quote: The plaster jacket containing the holotype of Effigia started to be prepared in 2004, and the specimen was uncovered by graduate student Sterling Nesbitt at the AMNH.
